Ltd. for nil consideration, the company said on October 4, 2026. The deal covers 3,84,04,205 equity shares of face value Rs 10 each and turns the 50:50 joint venture, incorporated in January 2008, into a wholly owned HAL subsidiary. HAL expects to close the share transfer within about 60 days of signing. The Ministry of Defence's Department of Defence Production has given administrative approval, with concurrence from the Department of Investment and Public Asset Management under the Ministry of Finance. HAL calls the deal a related-party transaction under SEBI listing rules and says it is not at arm's length, because HATSOFF is already half-owned by HAL.

HATSOFF trains helicopter pilots on simulators for the Indian Air Force, Army, Navy, Coast Guard and Border Security Force, plus civil customers including Pawan Hans and Global Vectra. Its turnover rose to Rs 80.95 crore in FY2025-26 from Rs 69.55 crore in FY2024-25 and Rs 66.49 crore in FY2023-24, about 16.4 per cent growth year on year, according to the article. That is less than 0.3 per cent of HAL's consolidated revenue from operations of Rs 33,088.82 crore in FY2025-26. HAL says the purchase secures full management control and streamlines decision-making, and it fits the company's push into helicopter manufacturing, maintenance, repair, overhaul and lifecycle support, including its greenfield helicopter project at Tumakuru.

The larger story for HAL is the Tejas Mk1A fighter, where a final review meeting with the Indian Air Force will be held after mid-October, a top defence official told TNIE. The review had been slated for September. Two or three minor issues remain with the Israeli EL/M-2052 AESA radar, which must mesh with the jet's weapon firing controls and its Angad electronic warfare suite. After that, the military airworthiness regulator CEMILAC must give final clearance. The first batch will go to Sulur in Tamil Nadu, home of the IAF's first Tejas Mk1 squadron, the Flying Daggers, and the first full Mk1A squadron will be raised at Nal in Rajasthan's Bikaner district, near the Pakistan border. The IAF expects to induct the first jets within this financial year.

HAL chairman Ravi K said last month that 27 Mk1A airframes were ready and 10 engines had been received from GE Aerospace, with one or two issues in the first batch needing more testing. He put the programme at 90-95 per cent complete. HAL's own target is to deliver the first squadron of 16-18 jets by March 2027. Engine supply is the other bottleneck: GE shipped three F404 engines in August, taking the total to 10. Former HAL chief D K Sunil said GE was committed to supplying 20 engines between June and December this year. HAL has imposed liquidated damages on GE for the delays, and the defence ministry has warned that HAL itself could face liquidated damages for missing its own delivery schedules.

The delays are large. Under the Rs 48,000 crore contract signed in February 2021 for 83 Tejas Mk1A jets, deliveries were to begin in February 2024. Not one jet has been delivered. The ministry then signed another Rs 62,370 crore contract for 97 more jets in September last year, taking the total to 180, and HAL signed a follow-on engine deal with GE for them. The IAF is down to 29 fighter squadrons, each with 16-18 jets, after retiring its MiG-21s, against a requirement of at least 42 to handle the combined threat from China and Pakistan.

On the transport side, Lockheed Martin is bidding for India's tender, issued in August, for 60 medium transport aircraft at a cost of USD 10.5 billion. Five Indian companies are in the fray: Tata Advanced Systems Limited (TASL), Mahindra Group, Adani Defence & Aerospace, HAL and Reliance Defence, each expected to bring in a global aircraft maker. TASL has partnered with Lockheed Martin; Mahindra has joined Brazil's Embraer. Dan Tenney, Lockheed Martin's senior vice president for global business development and strategy, said the company's existing C-130J component and empennage work with Tata would be expanded if the bid succeeds. Lockheed's proposal includes 12 aircraft in flyaway condition and 48 built in India, plus an upgrade of the IAF's 12 existing C-130Js to the same advanced configuration, which could give the force a common fleet of 72 aircraft. The current C-130J fleet has flown more than 58,000 hours, used for high-altitude operations in Ladakh, Nepal flood relief and the 2023 evacuation from Sudan.

What is still unconfirmed: the exact date of the Tejas review, whether the radar issues will be resolved without further slippage, and whether CEMILAC clearance follows quickly. HAL has not given a delivery date for the first Mk1A beyond the March 2027 squadron target. The HATSOFF deal is agreed but not closed, and the 60-day timeline is tentative. On the transport tender, no winner has been named, and Lockheed's expansion plans are conditional on winning.

The risks are concentrated in execution. Tejas Mk1A deliveries have slipped by more than two years against the February 2024 start, and the engine supply from GE remains behind schedule despite liquidated damages. Every further delay weakens the IAF's squadron count and raises the chance of penalties against HAL. The HATSOFF purchase is tiny in revenue terms and is a related-party deal at nil consideration, so it will not move group earnings; its value is control over pilot training as HAL sells and supports more helicopters. The medium transport aircraft bid is a contest HAL is in but does not control, and losing it would leave the expansion to a rival consortium.

What to watch next: the date and outcome of the IAF-HAL review after mid-October, CEMILAC's clearance, and any new GE engine shipments. Watch whether HAL confirms the first Mk1A delivery this financial year. Watch the 60-day HATSOFF share transfer. And watch the medium transport aircraft tender for the winning pair of an Indian company and a global manufacturer.

My view: the HATSOFF buyout is a small housekeeping move that adds control, not revenue. The Tejas Mk1A timeline is the material item, because 180 jets worth about Rs 1.1 lakh crore in total contract value sit behind a radar integration issue and a slow engine supplier, and that is what will decide HAL's earnings and the IAF's squadron strength over the next few years."}

The essay argues that human progress has always depended less on raw genius than on the machinery and bureaucracy needed to turn ideas into reality, and that AI is about to change which of those two things is scarce. The authors point to the James Webb Space Telescope: Galileo widened our view of the universe with two lenses and a tube, while Webb required eighteen mirror segments engineered to fifty nanometer precision, three hundred organizations across fourteen countries, and ten billion dollars. That gap is the point. Research productivity has been falling even as spending rises. Sustaining Moore's law now takes more than eighteen times as many researchers as it did in the early 1970s, and economy-wide research productivity fell by a factor of forty-one while research effort rose twenty-three-fold. The technician workforce is growing twice as fast as the scientists.

The authors call the unglamorous capacity to execute "institutional intelligence," and treat it as a complement to frontier intelligence: more of one raises the value of the other. Their bet is that AI will spend most of its time on the execution side, writing code, searching literature, turning sketches into prototypes. That would let one person pursue projects that once needed a whole organization, and push creative work outside the institutions that currently gatekeep it. The thing to watch is whether that produces a wave of independent work or just a new set of bottlenecks. My view: the essay is right that execution, not ideas, is the binding constraint, and that is exactly why the incumbents with the biggest bureaucracies stand to gain most.

Ltd. for nil consideration, turning the simulator training joint venture into a wholly owned subsidiary. The transaction covers 3,84,04,205 equity shares of face value Rs 10 each and is expected to close within 60 days of signing the share transfer agreement, according to Source 3. HAL has administrative approval from the Ministry of Defence's Department of Defence Production and concurrence from the Department of Investment and Public Asset Management under the Ministry of Finance. Because HAL is a state-controlled defence enterprise and the deal involves a foreign partner's stake, that government sign-off was required. HAL disclosed the transaction as a related-party transaction under SEBI's listing regulations, since HATSOFF is already a 50 per cent-owned joint venture, and said it is not at arm's length.

The numbers at HATSOFF are small next to HAL. The training venture's turnover rose to Rs 80.95 crore in FY2025-26 from Rs 69.55 crore in FY2024-25 and Rs 66.49 crore in FY2023-24, Source 3 reports, a gain of about 16.4 per cent year on year. HAL's consolidated revenue from operations was Rs 33,088.82 crore in FY2025-26, so HATSOFF accounted for less than 0.3 per cent of group revenue. HATSOFF has authorised capital of Rs 76.84 crore and paid-up capital of Rs 76.80 crore. It was incorporated in January 2008 as a 50:50 venture between HAL and CAE Canada, and trains helicopter pilots for the Indian Air Force, Army, Navy, Coast Guard and Border Security Force, plus civil customers including Pawan Hans and Global Vectra. HAL says full control will secure management control and streamline decision-making, and tie simulator training more closely to helicopter deliveries, fleet support and customer service. That fits HAL's wider push into helicopter manufacturing and lifecycle support, including its greenfield helicopter project at Tumakuru.

The larger story for HAL is the Tejas Mk1A fighter, where a final review meeting with the Indian Air Force will be held after mid-October, Source 2 reports. The meeting was earlier slated for September and will take place only when HAL brings its final update on pending issues; that assessment will decide the induction timeline, a senior defence official told TNIE. Most integration work is done, with two to three minor issues left in the jet's radar. The Israeli EL/M-2052 AESA radar, an active electronically scanned array that steers its beam electronically rather than by moving parts, must mesh with the jet's weapon firing controls and its Angad electronic warfare suite. After that, the jet still needs final clearance from CEMILAC, the military airworthiness regulator. The first batch will go to Sulur in Tamil Nadu, home of the IAF's first Tejas Mk1 squadron, and the first full Mk1A squadron will be raised at Nal in Rajasthan's Bikaner district, near the western front with Pakistan. The IAF expects to induct the first jets within this financial year.

HAL chairman Ravi K said last month that 27 Mk1A airframes were ready and 10 engines had been received from GE Aerospace, with one or two issues in the first batch needing more testing; he put the programme at 90-95 per cent complete. HAL's own target is to deliver the first squadron of 16-18 jets by March 2027. Engine supply from GE has been the other choke point. GE shipped three F404 engines in August, taking the total to 10. Former HAL chief D K Sunil said GE was committed to supplying 20 engines between June and December this year. HAL has imposed liquidated damages, a contractual penalty for late delivery, on GE, and the defence ministry has warned that HAL itself could face liquidated damages for missing its own schedules.

The delivery record is stark. Under the Rs 48,000 crore contract signed in February 2021 for 83 Tejas Mk1A jets, deliveries were to begin in February 2024. Not one jet has been delivered so far. The defence ministry signed a second contract for 97 more jets in September last year worth Rs 62,370 crore, taking the total to 180, and HAL signed a follow-on engine deal with GE for those aircraft. The shortfall matters because the IAF is down to 29 fighter squadrons, each with 16-18 jets, after retiring its MiG-21s, against a requirement of at least 42 to handle a threat from China and Pakistan together.

On the transport aircraft tender, Lockheed Martin says it would expand production in India if it wins the bid for 60 medium transport aircraft, valued at USD 10.5 billion, issued in August. Five Indian companies are in the running: Tata Advanced Systems Limited, Mahindra Group, Adani Defence & Aerospace, HAL and Reliance Defence, and each is expected to bring in a global aircraft maker. TASL has partnered with Lockheed Martin; Mahindra has tied up with Brazil's Embraer. Dan Tenney, Lockheed's senior vice president for global business development and strategy, said the company's existing work with Tata on C-130J components and empennages, the tail section of the aircraft, would be expanded in the current bid. Lockheed's proposal includes 12 aircraft in flyaway condition and 48 manufactured in India, plus an offer to upgrade the IAF's 12 existing C-130Js to the same advanced configuration, which could give the force a common fleet of 72 aircraft. The current C-130J fleet has flown more than 58,000 hours, used for high-altitude operations in Ladakh, Nepal flood relief and the 2023 evacuation from Sudan.

The Tejas review has no fixed date beyond "after mid-October", and the radar fixes, CEMILAC clearance and GE's engine deliveries all sit outside HAL's direct control. Whether Lockheed's India production plan becomes real depends on a bid outcome that has not been decided, and HAL is one of five contenders rather than the front-runner named in the reporting. The HATSOFF deal is approved but not yet closed; the 60-day window is the milestone to watch.

The risks are concentrated in execution. HAL is already exposed to penalties on Tejas if it misses schedules, and its supplier GE has been late. A further slip would delay a squadron the IAF needs and keep the fighter gap open. The transport tender is competitive and capital-intensive, and losing it would leave HAL without a role in a USD 10.5 billion programme. HATSOFF is too small to move group earnings, and buying a partner out for nil consideration raises governance questions that the related-party and non-arm's-length labels flag, even with government approval.

My view: the HATSOFF purchase is a minor housekeeping step that adds a recurring training service to HAL's helicopter business but changes little financially. {"headline": "Info Edge Ventures co-leads $15 million round in interior materials startup Gravity", "essay": "Info Edge Ventures has co-led a $15 million funding round in Gravity, a Bengaluru-based startup that supplies materials for home interiors. The round was co-led with 3one4 Capital, with Alteria Capital, Genesia Ventures and a group of angel investors also participating. Gravity raised the money as a mix of equity and debt, though it did not disclose the split between the two. The news was reported on 3 October 2026.

Info Edge Ventures is the venture capital arm of Info Edge, the listed Indian company that owns the job portal Naukri and stakes in several internet businesses. Info Edge is the parent that most readers of this briefing will know as Naukri's owner. The $15 million round is a small cheque by Info Edge's standards, but it is a fresh deployment of capital into a private company, and it tells you where the venture arm is putting money.

Gravity was founded by Saurabh Jain and Lalit Mittal, both former executives at Livspace, an Indian home interiors and renovation company. Jain was CEO for India at Livspace, where he helped scale the India business to an annualised revenue run rate of around Rs 1,500 crore. Mittal was chief business officer for India at Livspace and led its expansion across 30 cities. Earlier in his career, Jain co-founded DezignUp, a design community and marketplace that Livspace acquired in March 2015, after which he and other members of its core team joined Livspace.

Gravity describes itself as a platform for India's interior materials sector. It is initially focused on kitchens and wardrobes, bringing specialist businesses onto shared technology, distribution, procurement, key-account management and operating infrastructure. Its customers are designers, architects, modular showrooms and design-and-build studios, the people who select and procure materials for interior projects. The company says it wants to simplify a supply chain that remains fragmented across dealers, distributors and suppliers that each specialise in individual product categories. The platform is meant to improve availability, fulfilment and pricing visibility for those customers.

Gravity said the businesses in its initial portfolio have a combined revenue base running into several hundred crore rupees and are EBITDA positive. EBITDA is earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, a rough measure of operating profit. The company did not name the businesses in that portfolio, did not give a precise revenue figure, and did not say how many businesses are included. Those are gaps a reader should note.

The fresh capital will be used to strengthen technology, distribution and key-account infrastructure, expand into new categories, build the brand and support working capital as the company scales. Working capital is the cash a business needs for day-to-day operations, such as holding inventory and paying suppliers before customers pay. Gravity plans to expand into doors and windows, lighting, wall surfaces and home automation. It intends to use common technology, distribution and operating infrastructure across these categories rather than build separate systems for each business.

Why is this happening now? India's interior materials market is large and split among many dealers, distributors and category-specific suppliers. A platform that aggregates demand from designers and showrooms and offers shared back-end infrastructure can, in theory, get better prices from suppliers and better availability for customers. Gravity's founders have run a scaled interiors business before, which is the main reason investors are backing them at this stage. The venture arm of Info Edge has a history of backing consumer internet and marketplace businesses, and this fits that pattern.

What is still unknown is substantial. Gravity has not disclosed the equity-debt split, so the true cost of the capital and the dilution taken by existing shareholders are unclear. It has not named the businesses in its portfolio, so the claim of several hundred crore rupees in combined revenue and positive EBITDA cannot be checked. It has not said how many categories it will enter first or on what timeline. It has not said how the platform makes money, whether through commissions, subscriptions, or margin on materials sold. And it has not said how much of the $15 million is new money versus a structured debt facility from Alteria Capital, a specialist in venture debt.

For Info Edge, the risks here are the usual ones for a venture bet. The investment is small relative to the parent's overall business, so a poor outcome would not move the listed company's earnings much. But the interior materials supply chain is hard to change. Dealers and distributors have long-standing relationships, credit terms and local logistics. A platform that tries to insert itself between suppliers and buyers has to offer a clear reason for both sides to switch, and it has to do so across categories with different economics. Kitchens and wardrobes are project-based and involve measurement, customisation and installation. Lighting and home automation are more standardised but have their own specialist channels. Running all of them on shared infrastructure is the bet, and it is not yet proven.

There is also the question of competition. Livspace, where both founders worked, operates in the same broad space and has scale. Other players in building materials and home improvement have raised money and built distribution. Gravity's pitch is that it is a platform for materials rather than a consumer interiors brand, which puts it in a different lane, but the customers overlap.

What to watch next: whether Gravity names the businesses in its portfolio and gives a precise revenue figure; whether it discloses the equity-debt split; which new category it enters first and how quickly; and whether Info Edge Ventures participates in follow-on rounds. For the listed parent, the more important numbers remain those from Naukri and its other holdings, which report separately. This deal is a signal about where the venture arm sees opportunity, not a change to the earnings picture.

My view: this is a small, early-stage bet for Info Edge and it will not change the company's financial results in any meaningful way in the near term. Its value to a shareholder is as a read on the venture arm's judgment and on the founders' ability to build a platform business in a fragmented market, and that will take several years to judge."}

The offer itself is a fresh issue of up to 27 crore equity shares, equal to about 2.9% of the post-issue equity base. Sources put the raise at roughly $3.8 billion, or ₹36,100 crore, with one report citing about ₹37,700 crore. The price band is indicated at ₹1,300 to ₹1,450 per share. At the base end, that implies an enterprise valuation of $143-146 billion, or at least ₹12 lakh crore, according to banking sources cited by PTI. Other sources say the base valuation is expected above ₹13 lakh crore, with the upper end reaching ₹15 lakh crore if market conditions improve. The disagreement between sources is narrow but real: PTI's banking contacts describe a $143-146 billion base, while sources close to the preparations describe a ₹13-15 lakh crore range, which at current exchange rates is somewhat higher.

The proceeds will mostly go to Reliance Jio Infocomm, the telecom subsidiary, to repay or prepay borrowings. That matters because Jio Platforms carries the debt of a capital-intensive network build. The customer numbers show where growth is coming from. Total customers rose from 481.8 million in March 2024 to 488.2 million in March 2025 and 524.4 million in March 2026. Average revenue per user, the monthly bill per customer, rose from ₹181.7 in FY24 to ₹206.2 in FY25 and ₹214 in FY26. Monthly data consumption per customer hit 42.3 GB in the exit quarter of FY26, against 33.6 GB a year earlier. Total data traffic grew from 148.5 billion GB in FY24 to 241.4 billion GB in FY26. Fixed broadband connections exceeded 27 million. Jio's network carries about 60% of India's wireless data traffic, and the company holds 26,800.8 MHz of spectrum with an average remaining life of 16 years. It has over 360,000 network towers and more than one million route kilometres of fibre.

The valuation case rests on more than telecom. Jio Platforms reports over 336 million monthly digital subscriptions across entertainment, cloud and other services, and has filed more than 6,800 patent applications globally in areas including 4G, 5G, 6G and AI-driven network automation. Bankers are benchmarking the offer against Bharti Airtel, which has a market capitalisation of about ₹10.86 lakh crore. Sources say Jio could command at least a 20% premium to Airtel. That benchmark is being tested against a weak market: Airtel shares have fallen 17.2% in 2026 so far, the Nifty is down 14.2%, and Reliance Industries closed at ₹1,170 on October 1, down 25.7% this year. Sources say Jio has not seen a substantial decline in investor interest despite that backdrop.

Reliance Industries owns about 66.4% of Jio Platforms, and Meta and Google together hold about 17.7%, according to the draft prospectus. Meta invested ₹43,574 crore for 9.99% in 2020, and Google invested ₹33,737 crore for 7.73%. Other investors including Silver Lake, Vista Equity Partners, General Atlantic, KKR, Mubadala, Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, TPG, L Catterton, Intel Capital and Qualcomm Ventures collectively invested about ₹74,745 crore for roughly 15.2%. That is a third-party estimate, not company guidance.

The IPO also changes how the market values Jio: as a separately listed company, its telecom cash flows and digital bets will be judged on their own, without the conglomerate discount or cushion of Reliance Industries.

My view: the IPO is material less for the cash it raises, which is small relative to Jio's balance sheet, and more for what it does to the debt at Reliance Jio Infocomm and for the separate valuation the market will assign to the digital businesses. {"headline": "HAL Adds Shakti Engine Line, Closes Tejas Mk1 Order, Buys Out CAE Training Venture", "essay": "Hindustan Aeronautics Limited packed three separate developments into the first week of October 2026, and they point in the same direction: finishing old orders, adding capacity for new ones, and pulling a training joint venture fully in-house.

The most concrete number is ₹218 crore. That is the investment HAL is making in a second production line for the Shakti engine at its Koraput facility in Odisha. Defence Minister Rajnath Singh is scheduled to lay the foundation stone on Tuesday, 6 October 2026, according to the Ministry of Defence. The same event marks the delivery of Koraput's 2,000th aero-engine. Odisha Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi, Defence Production Secretary Sanjeev Kumar and HAL Chairman and Managing Director Ravi K are expected to attend.

The Shakti is a turboshaft engine, meaning it powers helicopters rather than fixed-wing jets. It is built through an Indo-French joint programme between HAL and Safran Helicopter Engines, and the new line will manufacture the Indian version of the Ardiden 1H1. The customers are the Dhruv Advanced Light Helicopter and the Prachand Light Combat Helicopter. Demand for those platforms just got much larger: the Ministry of Defence has signed contracts with HAL worth ₹62,700 crore for 156 Prachand helicopters, split as 66 for the Indian Air Force and 90 for the Army. Deliveries begin in the third year and run over five years. The government says it wants more than 65 per cent indigenous content during that contract, with more than 250 domestic companies, mostly small and medium enterprises, involved. The Prachand is designed to operate above 5,000 metres, which is why engine supply matters: thin air at altitude demands reliable power.

Koraput's history explains why the milestone is being treated as an event. The division opened in April 1964 building R11-F2/F2S turbojets for the MiG-21FL under licence, then moved through R25 and R29 engines for later MiG variants, RD-33 Series 3 engines for the MiG-29 from 2007-08, and AL-31FP engines for the Su-30MKI from 2004 under Russian licence. It has now built 2,000 engines and overhauled more than 7,700 aero-engines over five decades. In September 2024 the Defence Ministry signed a ₹26,000 crore contract for 240 AL-31FP engines, to be made at Koraput at 30 a year over eight years, with indigenous content rising to 63 per cent by the end of the programme and averaging above 54 per cent. In August this year HAL and Safran signed a final contract through their joint venture SAFHAL Helicopter Engines for the design, development, manufacture, supply and lifecycle support of the Aravalli, a 3,500 to 4,000 shaft horsepower turboshaft.

On the fighter side, HAL has fitted the last two twin-seat Tejas trainers from the original 2010 order with Israeli EL/M-2052 AESA radars and air-to-air refuelling probes. AESA stands for active electronically scanned array, a radar that steers its beam electronically instead of mechanically. The two aircraft, designated SPT7 and SPT8, close out the 40-jet Tejas Mk1 order placed in December 2010, which was split into 20 Initial Operational Clearance and 20 Final Operational Clearance aircraft, including four twin-seat trainers. Earlier trainers carried the older mechanically steered EL/M-2032 radar. The point of the upgrade is pilot transition: trainees will meet the sensor setup they will use in the Mk1A combat variant.

The Mk1A pipeline is where the volume sits. In 2021 the Ministry of Defence signed for 83 Tejas Mk1A aircraft, 73 single-seat fighters and 10 twin-seat trainers. In 2025 a follow-on order for 97 more Mk1A jets added 29 twin-seat trainers. Those 29 trainers are mandated to carry the domestically developed Uttam AESA radar and the Swayam Raksha Kavach electronic warfare suite as baseline equipment, replacing the imported Israeli avionics used on the aircraft just delivered. That is a genuine shift in the supply chain, not just a label.

The third item is small but tidy. HAL has agreed to acquire CAE Canada's 50 per cent stake in HATSOFF Helicopter Training, comprising 38,404,205 equity shares of ₹10 face value each, at nil consideration. HATSOFF runs military and civil helicopter pilot training on simulators. Once the shares transfer, expected within about 60 days of the share transfer agreement, HATSOFF becomes a wholly owned HAL subsidiary instead of a 50:50 joint venture. HAL's filing says the line of business aligns with its main business.

What is not yet known is how much of the new Shakti line's output is already contracted, and whether the ₹218 crore covers the full build-out or just the first phase. The articles give no delivery schedule for the second line, no capacity figure in engines per year, and no breakdown of how much of the Prachand's ₹62,700 crore value flows to HAL's engine division versus the airframe side. The nil-consideration transfer of the CAE stake also raises a question the filings do not answer: why CAE exited for nothing, and whether HAL is absorbing liabilities along with the shares.

The risks are the familiar ones for this business. Engine manufacturing under licence is not the same as designing an engine from scratch, and the articles quote N K Samal, a retired Indian Air Force official, saying India still lacks expertise in high-temperature materials, turbine technology, combustion systems, engine controls, and testing and certification. The Aravalli joint development with Safran is described as a bridge between licensed manufacturing and genuine joint development, which is a polite way of saying the hardest part is still ahead. On the Tejas side, the shift from Israeli to Indian radar and electronic warfare kit puts execution risk on domestic suppliers; any delay there feeds directly into the 97-aircraft order. And the Prachand contract's indigenous content target of over 65 per cent depends on hundreds of smaller suppliers delivering.

What to watch next: whether the second Shakti line gets a stated annual capacity and delivery schedule, whether the Uttam radar and Swayam Raksha Kavach suite stay on schedule for the 29 new trainers, and how quickly the HATSOFF share transfer closes within its 60-day window. The stock traded at ₹4,648.90 on the BSE on 5 October 2026, up 0.74 per cent, with a market capitalisation of ₹310,712.87 crore and promoter holding of 71.64 per cent, according to Accord Fintech.

My view: the Shakti line is the most material item here because it adds physical capacity against a ₹62,700 crore helicopter order that already exists, while the Tejas trainer upgrade is a tidy close-out of a 2010 contract rather than new revenue. The HATSOFF buyout is housekeeping, but it does put simulator training revenue and capability fully inside HAL rather than shared with a partner."}

The Shakti is a turboshaft engine, meaning it drives a helicopter's rotor rather than a jet's thrust. HAL builds 80 Ardiden 1H1 Shakti engines a year at its Bengaluru plant today. The Koraput line lifts annual capacity to 180 engines, the officials said. The engine was co-developed with Safran of France and powers the Dhruv advanced light helicopter and the Prachand light combat helicopter.

The demand case behind the extra capacity is a Ministry of Defence order worth ₹62,700 crore for 156 Prachand helicopters, split as 66 for the Indian Air Force and 90 for the Army. Deliveries start in the third year and run five years, per the Economic Times. The government wants more than 65% of the Prachand contract executed with Indian content, with over 250 domestic suppliers, mostly small and medium firms, involved. The Prachand is built for high-altitude operations above 5,000 metres.

The 2,000th engine itself was an AL-31FP, the powerplant for the Sukhoi-30MKI fighter. Koraput has made engines under Russian licence since 1964, starting with the R11-F2/F2S for the MiG-21FL, then the R25 for the MiG-21BIS, the R29B for the MiG-27M, and from 2007-08 the RD-33 Series 3 for the MiG-29. In September 2024 the Defence Ministry signed a ₹26,000 crore contract with HAL for 240 AL-31FP engines, to be built at Koraput at 30 a year over eight years. Indigenous content averages above 54% across that programme and reaches 63% in the final lot, with only some spares, forgings and castings imported. The IAF flies 260 Su-30s and will get 12 more to replace aircraft lost in accidents; HAL estimates the fleet will need around 900 engines over its lifetime. That is a long revenue tail, though it is spread over many years.

AESA means an electronically scanned radar with no moving antenna. Earlier trainers carried the older mechanically steered EL/M-2032. The 2010 order was split into 20 Initial Operational Clearance and 20 Final Operational Clearance aircraft, including four twin-seaters. With these two done, HAL says it can focus on the Mk1A line.

The Mk1A pipeline is large. A 2021 contract covered 83 aircraft, 73 single-seat fighters and 10 twin-seat trainers. A 2025 follow-on added 97 jets, including 29 trainers. The reports also do not say when the first Prachand airframes will be ready to receive engines, so the link between the new line and the ₹62,700 crore contract is a capacity claim, not a booked revenue figure.

The Tejas Mk1A delivery count for this year rests on the chairman's stated confidence and 10 engines received, not on a signed-off schedule.
